power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: The plurality of metacognition: Historical origins and research traditions

text.text: Metacognition is commonly defined as the monitoring and control of one's own cognition, yet the term covers related phenomena that differ in their theoretical organisation, assessment, and application.
This historically oriented narrative review examines how the convergence of cognitive, developmental, and educational research traditions produced this plurality.

It reconstructs the construct's empirical and theoretical antecedents in memory monitoring, children's knowledge of cognition, and strategic regulation of learning, and compares influential accounts in terms of their explanatory aims, central components, and levels of analysis.

The comparison shows that different traditions came to emphasise metacognitive knowledge, experiences, monitoring, regulatory activity, or the functional relation between object-and metalevel cognition.
These differences are interpreted not as competing definitions of an identical phenomenon, but as reflecting the distinct problems and methods from which each account developed.

The review argues that metacognition is best approached as a historically assembled family of related but partially non-interchangeable facets, without assuming either complete unity or fragmentation.

This interpretation clarifies why indicators derived from different traditions often diverge, and why specifying the facet, function, and level of analysis intended by the term should be a condition for cumulative research across theory, measurement, and application.
Metacognition refers to the human capacity to monitor and control one's own cognitive processes (Nelson & Narens, 1990).
text.formatted: Metacognition refers to the human capacity to monitor and control one's own cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Nelson & Narens, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: It is involved in a wide range of everyday activities, including evaluating whether we have understood a text (Yang et al., 2023), acting and communicating with others (Heyes et al., 2020), pursuing short-and long-term goals (Scott & Gilbert, 2024), and making decisions (Basu & Dixit, 2022).
text.formatted: It is involved in a wide range of everyday activities, including evaluating whether we have understood a text <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Yang et al., 2023)</ref>, acting and communicating with others <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Heyes et al., 2020)</ref>, pursuing short-and long-term goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Scott & Gilbert, 2024)</ref>, and making decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Basu & Dixit, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Metacognition has consequently become a central construct in cognitive, developmental, and educational psychology (Norman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Metacognition has consequently become a central construct in cognitive, developmental, and educational psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Norman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Yet this apparently straightforward definition conceals a conceptually plural field.

Researchers use the term metacognition to refer to partially overlapping phenomena, including knowledge about cognition, the monitoring of cognitive activity, feelings of knowing, confidence judgements, learning strategies, planning, and regulatory control (Dunlosky & Metcalfe, 2009).
text.formatted: Researchers use the term metacognition to refer to partially overlapping phenomena, including knowledge about cognition, the monitoring of cognitive activity, feelings of knowing, confidence judgements, learning strategies, planning, and regulatory control <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dunlosky & Metcalfe, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Although related, these phenomena do not necessarily involve the same processes, operate at the same level of analysis, or serve the same explanatory purposes.
This plurality is not merely a product of inconsistent contemporary terminology.
It also reflects the historical convergence of distinct research programmes that originally addressed different psychological questions (Brown et al., 1983).
text.formatted: It also reflects the historical convergence of distinct research programmes that originally addressed different psychological questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental research in cognitive psychology examined how individuals assess the accessibility and accuracy of their memory processes (Hart, 1965; Nelson, 1984).
text.formatted: Experimental research in cognitive psychology examined how individuals assess the accessibility and accuracy of their memory processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Hart, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Nelson, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Developmental researchers investigated children's growing understanding of language and memory, and their use of strategies to regulate learning (Flavell et al., 1966 (Flavell et al., , 1970;; Gleitman et al., 1972).
text.formatted: Developmental researchers investigated children's growing understanding of language and memory, and their use of strategies to regulate learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Flavell et al., 1966</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Flavell et al., , 1970;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Gleitman et al., 1972)</ref>.

text.text: In educational psychology, researchers focused on how metacognitive knowledge and regulatory strategies could be elicited, observed, and taught in meaningful activities such as reading comprehension and problem solving in educational contexts (Baker & Brown, 1984; Brown, 1978; Palincsar & Brown, 1984).
text.formatted: In educational psychology, researchers focused on how metacognitive knowledge and regulatory strategies could be elicited, observed, and taught in meaningful activities such as reading comprehension and problem solving in educational contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baker & Brown, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brown, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Palincsar & Brown, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Although these programmes eventually came to share the label metacognition, they originated in different empirical problems and developed partly distinct concepts, methods, and explanatory aims.
These different origins shaped how the construct was theoretically organised.

Some accounts focused on the knowledge and conscious experiences involved in monitoring one's own cognition (Flavell, 1979); others emphasised the executive processes through which cognitive activity is planned, monitored, and regulated (Brown et al., 1983); still others proposed functional architectures that link object-level cognitive activity to meta-level representations (Nelson & Narens, 1990).
text.formatted: Some accounts focused on the knowledge and conscious experiences involved in monitoring one's own cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Flavell, 1979)</ref>; others emphasised the executive processes through which cognitive activity is planned, monitored, and regulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 1983)</ref>; still others proposed functional architectures that link object-level cognitive activity to meta-level representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Nelson & Narens, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Later frameworks sought to integrate these perspectives by distinguishing relatively stable metacognitive knowledge, task-related metacognitive experiences, and regulatory metacognitive skills, while specifying how these facets interact across levels of functioning (Efklides, 2008).
text.formatted: Later frameworks sought to integrate these perspectives by distinguishing relatively stable metacognitive knowledge, task-related metacognitive experiences, and regulatory metacognitive skills, while specifying how these facets interact across levels of functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Efklides, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These approaches therefore represent more than alternative models of an otherwise identical phenomenon: they retain different assumptions about what metacognition comprises, how its components relate to one another, and what a theory of metacognition is intended to explain.

Contemporary reviews have documented the breadth of metacognition and the diversity of definitions, models, and methods used to study it (e.g., Azevedo, 2020; Fleur et al., 2021; Norman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Contemporary reviews have documented the breadth of metacognition and the diversity of definitions, models, and methods used to study it (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Azevedo, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Fleur et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Norman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, these accounts are typically organised around present-day conceptual distinctions, measurement approaches, or applications.
Comparatively less attention has been paid to reconstructing how the construct's early research traditions shaped the later development of its theoretical models.

A historically informed account can therefore clarify not only when particular concepts and models emerged, but also why different traditions came to emphasise particular components, levels of analysis, and explanatory questions.
This article presents a historically oriented narrative review of the origins and theoretical traditions that shaped metacognition into a plural construct.

It has three aims: (i) to identify the principal empirical and theoretical antecedents of the construct; (ii) to compare influential accounts developed within cognitive, developmental, and educational research traditions; and (iii) to examine how differences in those traditions' historical origins continue to shape what is understood as metacognition.

The first section reconstructs the lines of research that preceded the formal introduction of the construct, from early studies of memory monitoring and strategic behaviour to the emergence of the concepts of metamemory and metacognition.

The second section examines influential theoretical models and compares how each defines, organises, and explains metacognitive activity, and shows that each model's emphasis is traceable to the empirical problems its parent tradition had made observable.

The final section draws out the implications of this historically grounded plurality: it argues that the divergence among contemporary indicators and the contested boundaries of the construct are consequences of the traditions from which models and instruments descend, and that specifying the facet, function, and level of analysis intended by the term is a condition for cumulative research across theory, measurement, and application.
The study of metacognition, also known as "cognition about cognition" (Flavell, 1985, p. 104), has deep roots in both philosophy and psychology (Lyons, 1986).

text.text: The idea that the mind can "turn back" upon its own operations has a long philosophical history, appearing in reflections on introspection and consciousness long before the emergence of scientific psychology (Schwitzgebel, 2024).
text.formatted: The idea that the mind can "turn back" upon its own operations has a long philosophical history, appearing in reflections on introspection and consciousness long before the emergence of scientific psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Schwitzgebel, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Its psychological antecedents can be traced to authors such as William James (1890/2016), John Dewey (1910 Dewey ( /2009)), Edward Thorndike (1913 ), and Charles Spearman (1927 /2022), yet the formal investigation of this idea only began during the so-called cognitive renaissance of the late 1950s and early 1960s (Bruner et al., 1956; Miller et al., 1960).

text.text: After behaviourism, characterised by the predominance of stimulus-response explanations, cognitivism emerged, placing the mind and cognitive processes once again at the centre of psychology (Miller, 2003).
text.formatted: After behaviourism, characterised by the predominance of stimulus-response explanations, cognitivism emerged, placing the mind and cognitive processes once again at the centre of psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Miller, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its uneven impact in both American and European psychology (Brock, 2013), this movement provided the conditions for psychologists on both sides of the Atlantic to ask how individuals know about their own mental activity: how they monitor it, how much they know about it, and how they use that knowledge (Baker & Brown, 1984; Lyons, 1986).
text.formatted: Despite its uneven impact in both American and European psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brock, 2013)</ref>, this movement provided the conditions for psychologists on both sides of the Atlantic to ask how individuals know about their own mental activity: how they monitor it, how much they know about it, and how they use that knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baker & Brown, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lyons, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Within this context, metacognition came to be understood as the monitoring and control of one's own mental processes (Flavell, 1979).
text.formatted: Within this context, metacognition came to be understood as the monitoring and control of one's own mental processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Flavell, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: One of the earliest empirical attempts to study how individuals monitor their own cognition was conducted by Joseph Hart (1965) in his study of feeling-of-knowing experiences, understood as an individual's belief that, despite being unable to retrieve certain information at a given moment, they would be able to recognise it later. Hart (1965) set out to evaluate whether these beliefs are precise indicators of the real contents of a person's memory, seeking evidence of a self-monitoring mechanism over it.

text.text: To this end, he applied a single-answer general information questionnaire to a group of individuals.
If they did not know a correct answer, they were instructed to judge whether they could identify it from a list of options.

Finally, to evaluate the accuracy of these judgements, the participants had to answer a second questionnaire with the same questions they could not initially answer, but this time with multiple-choice questions.

The results showed that performance on the multiple-choice questionnaire was better when participants had prospectively indicated that they believed they could identify the correct answer from a list of options than when they thought they could not.
These findings suggested that people could monitor the accessibility of information in their own memory, even when they could not retrieve it.

These findings, on what Hart (1967) termed the memory monitoring process, constituted a turning point in memory research and were even considered by some as the future of the discipline (Tulving & Madigan, 1970).
text.formatted: These findings, on what <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Hart (1967)</ref> termed the memory monitoring process, constituted a turning point in memory research and were even considered by some as the future of the discipline <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Tulving & Madigan, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: In the following years, researchers extended the experimental study of related phenomena involving memory monitoring and learning.

These included tip-of-thetongue states, first examined experimentally by Brown and McNeill (1966), though originally described by James (1890/2016) and later discussed by Woodworth (1934); ease-of-learning judgements, defined as the ability to judge how easy or difficult a particular material will be to learn (Underwood, 1966); and judgements of learning, defined as the ability to prospectively evaluate the likelihood that studied information will be remembered later (Arbuckle & Cuddy, 1969).

text.text: Collectively, these studies pointed in the same direction as Hart's (1965) findings: individuals can monitor their own cognition, and, although this ability is far from perfect, their judgements are systematically related to subsequent memory performance.

text.text: In a study on recognition memory, they observed that when a word feels unfamiliar, participants can correctly reject it as "new" almost instantly.
These rapid negative responses were significantly faster than what would be expected if participants had to mentally search through an entire memorised list of words.
Later work by Kolers and Palef (1976) provided further evidence that memory monitoring may operate independently of an exhaustive search process.

text.text: These results provided a basis for distinguishing between the retrieval of stored information and the processes through which individuals assess its accessibility.

In parallel with cognitive research on memory monitoring in adults, developmental research focused on children's use of strategies to regulate learning and memory performance (Daehler et al., 1969; Hagen et al., 1970).

text.text: Earlier developmental theories had already addressed processes that would later become central to metacognition.

Piaget examined how children progressively move beyond egocentric thought to coordinate perspectives, reflect on rules, and develop increasingly organised forms of reasoning (Piaget, 1926 (Piaget, /1959)), whereas Vygotsky described how externally mediated verbal regulation could become self-directed speech and, eventually, inner speech (Vygotsky, 1934 (Vygotsky, /2020)).

text.text: One of the researchers who stood out in this period was John H. Flavell, whose earlier work had helped introduce Piagetian developmental theory to anglophone psychology.

Situated within developmental debates shaped by the work of Piaget and Vygotsky on self-regulation in children, Flavell et al. (1966) studied children's use of spontaneous verbal rehearsal through a memorybased experimental paradigm.
text.formatted: Situated within developmental debates shaped by the work of Piaget and Vygotsky on self-regulation in children, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Flavell et al. (1966)</ref> studied children's use of spontaneous verbal rehearsal through a memorybased experimental paradigm.

text.text: They found that second and fifth grade children not only performed better than kindergarteners but also presented more spontaneous verbal production during the task.
These verbalisations were far from accidental: children used them to improve their ability to remember the pictured items, thereby regulating their performance.
Moreover, children who engaged in verbal rehearsal were not only aware of their strategy use but also of its specific purpose.

Subsequent studies continued to explore the use of verbalisation as a strategy for enhancing children's performance on memorisation tasks (e.g., Hagen & Kingsley, 1968; Keeney et al., 1967; Kingsley & Hagen, 1969). Flavell et al. (1970) identified a relationship between the use of self-regulation strategies and memory monitoring.

(1970)</ref> identified a relationship between the use of self-regulation strategies and memory monitoring.

text.text: In a study with 84 children from kindergarten to fourth grade, they demonstrated not only that older children were capable of using relatively complex memorisation strategies but also that, compared to younger children, they were better at predicting their own memory capacity and judging whether they had memorised a list of words well enough for later recall.
These findings suggested that successful memorisation -in this case, of a word list-was predicted by the use of more effective learning strategies.

This strategic competence, in turn, was closely related to the knowledge and awareness that children had regarding how their own memory worked or, as Tulving and Madigan described it a few months earlier, "knowledge of their own knowledge" (1970, p. 477).

text.text: Thus, Flavell et al. (1970) provided early empirical evidence that cognitive monitoring and self-regulatory learning strategies are fundamentally related.

text.text: The consolidation of research on cognitive monitoring and self-regulation strategies found a point of convergence at the 1971 symposium of the Society for Research in Child Development, where Flavell first coined the concept of metamemory.

This construct, defined as the different storage and retrieval strategies an individual uses alongside the intelligent monitoring and knowledge about those strategies (Flavell, 1971), provided a bridge towards the formal study of metacognitive processes in psychology (Dunlosky & Tauber, 2016; Ornstein & Haden, 2001; Rhodes, 2019).

text.text: These lines examined how people know about and monitor other cognitive processes and how such abilities develop in childhood.

As noted by Brown (1978) and Flavell (1976), the intellectual climate of the 1960s and 1970s fostered the proliferation of many "metas", that is, neologisms using the prefix meta (from the Greek μετά, "after") to "elevate the original meaning of such a word to a higher, more abstract philosophical level" (Thomas, 1984, p. 16).

text.text: In 1972, Gleitman and colleagues captured this zeitgeist and summarised it in a single word: "metacognition".

While studying the emergence of grammatical reasoning in children -what we call today metalinguistic knowledge or awareness-, Gleitman et al. (1972) coined the concept of metacognition and referred for the first time to "meta-cognitive" processes to describe a series of higher-order psychological processes that have as their object other cognitive processes, such as memory, "as if the homunculus perceived the operations of a lower-order system" (p. 161).

text.text: They drew explicit parallels between how we can reflect "meta-linguistically" and similar processes in memory such as recollection, intentional learning, and the "tip-of-the-tongue" phenomenon.
In their view, metacognition marked the capacity not only to use cognitive functions like memory or language but also to recognise and reflect upon their operation.

They further noted developmental evidence suggesting that such skills typically emerge close to the five-to-seven-year age range, a period consistent with broader advances in children's reasoning abilities (Ginsburg & Opper, 1969; Yendovitskaya, 1971).

text.text: Although this early use of the term has received considerably less attention than Flavell's later formulation, it was the first to conceptualise metacognition as a phenomenon extending beyond memory monitoring and into multiple cognitive domains.
The term acquired wider recognition a few years later, when John Flavell provided its first widely recognised definition.
In a brief chapter entitled Metacognitive aspects of problem solving, Flavell (1976) highlighted the relevance of metacognition for intelligent behaviour and problem-solving.
text.formatted: In a brief chapter entitled Metacognitive aspects of problem solving, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Flavell (1976)</ref> highlighted the relevance of metacognition for intelligent behaviour and problem-solving.

text.text: In this chapter, Flavell defined it as "one's own knowledge concerning one's own cognitive processes and products or anything related to them, e.g., the learning-relevant properties of information or data" (p. 232), and added that "metacognition refers, among other things, to the active monitoring and consequent regulation and orchestration of these processes in relation to the cognitive objects or data on which they bear" (p. 232).

According to the author, metacognition functions as a source of regulatory control that allows the individual not only to determine how, where, and when to use available regulatory strategies but also to be aware of those strategies themselves.

Flavell's definition brought together two functions that had become increasingly prominent across these lines of research: knowledge and monitoring of cognition, on the one hand, and the active regulation of cognitive processes, on the other.

This formulation established a central distinction for the literature, still relevant today, where metacognition involves both representations or judgements about cognition and processes through which cognitive activity is monitored and regulated (Boldt & Gilbert, 2022; Craig et al., 2020; Fleur et al., 2021; Tarricone, 2011; Veenman et al., 2006; Winne & Azevedo, 2014).

text.text: These longstanding tensions laid the foundation for the different theoretical models that emerged in the literature, each shaped by the goals and assumptions of its respective research tradition.
The theoretical models that followed organised the emerging construct in different ways, reflecting the empirical inquiries of their respective research traditions.
One of the first systematic attempts to organise the construct of metacognition can be found in Flavell and Wellman's (1977) work on metamemory.

text.text: In that paper, the authors proposed that children gradually acquired knowledge about their own memory processes along two dimensions: (i) sensitivity to situations in which deliberate memory-related efforts are needed, and (ii) knowledge about the factors that influence memory performance, namely, person, task, and strategy variables, as well as their interactions.

Critically, they distinguished two functionally distinct forms of metamemory: a general, previously acquired knowledge about the self and others as mnemonic agents, and a more immediate, situational ability to "monitor and interpret concrete experiences in the here and now" (Flavell & Wellman, 1977, p. 18).

text.text: Following this work, Flavell (1979) expanded the scope of metamemory into a broader theory of metacognition.

text.text: In his seminal work, he described four classes of phenomena through whose actions and interactions cognitive monitoring occurs (see Figure 1A): metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals (or tasks), and actions (or strategies).
text.formatted: In his seminal work, he described four classes of phenomena through whose actions and interactions cognitive monitoring occurs (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>): metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals (or tasks), and actions (or strategies).

text.text: Metacognitive knowledge refers to what individuals know and believe about themselves and others as cognitive agents, about the different types of tasks they perform, and about the strategies they use for learning or remembering -categories that echo the person, task, and strategy variables in his earlier work with Wellman.
Metacognitive experiences, in turn, correspond to the conscious cognitive and affective events that precede, accompany, or follow any cognitive enterprise.
Finally, goals and actions refer respectively to the objectives of such enterprises and to the cognitions or behaviours used to achieve them.

According to this model, cognitive monitoring occurs through the continuous interactions among these four phenomena: metacognitive knowledge provides the basis for interpreting one's cognitive activity, metacognitive experiences provide conscious information about its course and outcomes, and goals and strategies guide its direction and adjustment.

Although Flavell (1979) did not describe regulation as a distinct component, his model clearly implied it: both metacognitive knowledge and experiences were conceived as mechanisms through which the individual can select, activate, evaluate, revise, and abandon goals and strategies in order to accomplish a cognitive enterprise.

text.text: Alongside Flavell's formulations, Ann L. Brown played a pivotal role in consolidating the study of metacognition and bringing it closer to educational contexts.
Brown, however, placed greater emphasis on the executive and regulatory functions of metacognitive activity.

As Reder (1996) points out, the processes she labelled as metacognitive skills (Brown, 1978; Brown et al., 1983), such as planning, monitoring and evaluating, had already been discussed in earlier theories of executive control and processing.

text.text: In contrast, metacognitive experiences correspond to the online, affect-and cognitive-based signals -such as feelings of difficulty, knowing, or confidence-that arise during task engagement and provide feedback about the course of cognitive processing (Efklides, 2001 (Efklides, , 2008)).

text.text: Finally, metacognitive skills refer to the deliberate control processes involved in planning, monitoring, and evaluating one's actions (Efklides, 2006). Efklides (2008) further organised these facets within a multilevel structure that distinguishes a nonconscious object level, comprising cognition and emotion, as well as their respective regulatory systems, and a meta level at which explicit awareness, monitoring, and regulatory decisions take place.

text.text: At this level, the three facets of metacognition operate in coordination, with metacognitive knowledge and experiences informing the deployment of metacognitive skills to guide regulation.
Efklides also acknowledged a broader social level of functioning, involving the monitoring and regulation of others' cognition in interactive contexts.

Although this framework offers a coherent account of how metacognitive components interact during learning, it also illustrates how different theoretical traditions emphasise distinct facets and levels of analysis within the broader construct of metacognition.

text.text: These models therefore overlap in their subject matter without being interchangeable: they are emphases, not exclusive territories, and the history of the field is not a developmental sequence culminating in one superior model (Norman et al., 2019; Veenman et al., 2006).

text.text: This comparison also clarifies why the differences among the models are not accidental.

Each model was developed to answer an empirical question that its parent tradition had already made tractable: memory-monitoring experiments made confidence and feeling-of-knowing judgements measurable; developmental strategy research made the emergence of knowledge about cognition observable; classroom pedagogy and assessment made strategic regulation observable in authentic tasks; and functional-architecture research made the monitoring-control relation formalisable.
A model's emphasis is therefore not a free theoretical choice but is conditioned by the empirical problem it was built to solve.
The consequence of this history is that the boundaries of what counts as metacognition are still drawn differently depending on which tradition a researcher is working within.

The same behaviour (a student pausing to reconsider a strategy, a participant reporting confidence in a memory judgement, a child explaining why a strategy worked) is classified as metacognitive knowledge, as monitoring, as regulation, or as strategy use depending on the framework brought to bear (Dörrenbächer-Ulrich & Bregulla, 2024; Veenman et al., 2006).

text.text: Because those classifications are theory-laden rather than self-evident, they shape what counts as evidence, what counts as a metacognitive failure, and what an intervention is meant to change.

Whether this plurality should be read as a defect of the construct or as a condition of its productivity, and what follows from it for theory, measurement, and application, is the question taken up in the final section.
The three aims of this review point to the same conclusion.
The first section showed that metacognition did not emerge from a single research programme but from several, each of which was addressing a different empirical problem (Brown et al., 1983).
text.formatted: The first section showed that metacognition did not emerge from a single research programme but from several, each of which was addressing a different empirical problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: The second section showed that each model built the construct around the phenomena its own tradition was able to observe.
Different facets became central, in other words, for empirical reasons before they became matters of definition.
The third aim follows from the first two.
Because these emphases survive in current models and instruments, they still shape not only how metacognition is labelled but what counts as evidence of it.

Metacognition is therefore best understood as a historically assembled family of related but partially non-interchangeable facets, rather than as a single, settled construct (Dunlosky & Metcalfe, 2009; Norman et al., 2019).

text.text: This does not mean that the facets are independent, or that common mechanisms cannot be found.

Task-based metacognition shows both shared and domain-specific components, which warns against replacing the assumption of complete unity with an equally sweeping assumption of fragmentation (Lehmann et al., 2022).

text.text: Nor does plurality make the construct useless.

Its value as an umbrella term lies in connecting questions about cognition as something that can be known, experienced, monitored, and controlled, as long as the intended meaning is made explicit (Norman et al., 2019).

text.text: The historical account also helps to make sense of a familiar methodological problem.

Self-report inventories, verbal protocols, and task-based indicators of metacognition often correlate weakly or inconsistently with one another (Craig et al., 2020; Terneusen et al., 2024; Zepeda & Nokes-Malach, 2023), and their associations with academic achievement depend on which measure is used (Dent & Koenka, 2016; Ohtani & Hisasaka, 2018).

text.text: Seen historically, this is not surprising.
Inventories such as the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory descend from Brown's distinction between knowledge and regulation of cognition; they were designed to make teachable skills reportable.
Confidence-based indices descend from the memory-monitoring experiments of Hart and Nelson; they were designed to quantify how accurately people judge their own performance.

Each kind of instrument inherits its lineage's assumptions about what metacognition is and how it can be accessed. Brown et al. (1983) themselves noted that regulation depends on the situation and is not always open to conscious report.

text.text: This argument does not, however, exempt instruments from validity testing. Double (2025) found that self-reported monitoring ability was negatively associated with several online indices of monitoring, and that higher self-ratings went together with greater confidence and poorer performance.

text.text: Findings of this kind call into question whether such scores measure monitoring at all; they are not simply another example of legitimate differences between facets.
The appropriate conclusion is therefore conditional.
Divergence between measures does not automatically invalidate one of them, nor does it establish that they measure distinct constructs.
What it requires is scrutiny of what each measure was built to capture and of its methodological properties (Craig et al., 2020).

text.text: Conceptually, the same history explains why specifying the facet, function, and level of analysis one has in mind is not a terminological nicety but a condition for interpreting findings across traditions. text.text: Integrative accounts can make these relations explicit without settling the construct's boundaries. Efklides and Schwartz (2024), revisiting the Metacognitive and Affective model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL), distinguish person-level characteristics from task-specific functioning.

text.text: This offers a way to study relations across levels; it does not provide grounds for equating metacognition with the wider system in which it participates.
Strategy use or executive control should therefore not be taken as evidence of metacognition in general unless that inference is justified.
The same requirement applies to applied research, where education has been the main testing ground.

Janssen and Lazonder's (2024) meta-analysis illustrates the specificity required: its evidence concerns absolute monitoring accuracy in problem solving, and the effects depended on the type of intervention.
An improvement in one facet should not be reported as an improvement in metacognition as such.

Likewise, evaluations should distinguish evidence that the targeted facet changed from evidence that learning improved and should examine the link between the two rather than infer one from the other.
These conclusions have limits.
As a narrative comparison of selected traditions, the review cannot determine the empirical structure of metacognition or settle every proposed relation among its facets.
What it offers is a historical account of why those relations are contested.
The reconstruction is also selective in a second sense.
It follows the Anglo-American lines of research from which the dominant models descend and pays less attention to traditions that developed alongside or after them.

These include the German research on metacognition and motivation represented in the Weinert and Kluwe (1987) volume; the later development of the memorymonitoring lineage into a signal-detection and neuroscientific research programme on confidence (Fleming, 2024), whose current methods this review draws on but whose history it does not reconstruct; and accounts of the social and cultural origins of metacognition (Heyes et al., 2020).

text.text: Each would add further facets, and perhaps further lineages, to the family described here.

One direction for future work is to extend the historical reconstruction to these traditions and to the decades in which the construct moved from developmental and educational psychology into cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology, and comparative research.

Another is to use the lineages identified here as an analytical tool: mapping current instruments and intervention targets onto the tradition whose assumptions they inherit would make it possible to predict, rather than merely observe, where they converge and where they diverge.
More than four decades ago, Brown et al. (1983) described metacognition as a many-headed monster of obscure parentage.

text.text: Its parentage can now be reconstructed.
The heads of the monster correspond to research traditions that asked different questions about cognition as an object of cognition and built the methods needed to answer them.
The construct's characteristic difficulties in definition, measurement, and application follow from the same historical pluralism that made it productive in the first place.
Progress does not depend on agreement about a single encompassing framework.
It can proceed through clearer statements of what is being explained, measures that fit those claims, and applications whose scope matches the evidence.
Understood historically, the plurality of metacognition becomes interpretable, without the expectation that it must disappear.
